speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: asked the Minister for Health regarding exceptional cases where patients urgently require drugs that are not within HSA’s approved list (a) how can the Ministry assist these patients who require non-standard treatment options to qualify for claims under the current health insurance policy; (b) whether the Ministry will consider setting up a national body where medical experts can be swiftly mobilised to consider and approve these requests; and (c) how often does the list of approved drugs get updated to keep pace with medical advances.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) how many cancer patients will be affected by the new policy that limits insurance coverage for outpatient cancer drug treatments; (b) what is the recourse for patients who do not respond to these drugs; and (c) how often will the list of drugs be reviewed to ensure that it stays abreast with medical developments, especially new and rare cancers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The current claim limit that is applied to all types of cancer drugs gives pharmaceutical companies little or no reason to lower prices and takes away the Government’s negotiating power.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This has resulted in an unsustainable rise of cancer drug prices.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If left unchecked, cancer drugs will, eventually, be unaffordable for the majority of cancer patients.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The changes, focusing MediShield Life and Integrated Shield Plans (IPs) to cover a Cancer Drug List (CDL) of clinically-proven and more cost-effective cancer drug treatments, improve affordability in two ways.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: First, it provides the incentive for pharmaceutical companies to price their drugs more reasonably so as to benefit from financing coverage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The lower prices have made more cancer drugs cost-effective, enabling 66 more cancer drugs to be listed for subsidy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Second, nudging utilisation of cancer drugs towards proven and cost-effective care will ensure that treatment costs for the broad majority do not rise unsustainably as a result of liberal use of very expensive and novel cancer drugs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These changes will benefit thousands of patients and improve affordability of more cancer drugs for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We already have a panel of experts, comprising senior public and private oncologists and haematologists across various specialisations, who recommend new treatments for inclusion into CDL.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This panel has approved treatments that cover multiple lines of therapy, beyond first line treatment, as well as rare cancer treatments to CDL.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This has allowed us to include around 50 more treatments into CDL since it was announced in August 2021.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, we note that there could be exceptions where patients do not respond to treatments on CDL and their doctors may exercise clinical discretion to prescribe non-CDL treatments based on evidence of benefit.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In these cases, doctors must be prepared to justify their clinical decisions to patients and their colleagues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Doctors must also counsel the patient on its risks, efficacy and costs so that the patient may make an informed choice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Some patients may still be covered for such non-CDL treatments by their private insurance, such as riders or critical illness plans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Private patients who have difficulty affording their bills may opt to be transferred to subsidised care at public healthcare institutions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Once patients are in subsidised care, they can benefit from more affordable drugs and medical fees, as well as access a range of financial assistance, such as MediFund.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: All patients can also appeal to use more MediSave.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What actions are taken against this company for profiteering?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: My second supplementary question is on patients who have rare cancers and are requiring those drugs which are not on the list currently.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is there a mechanism for them to appeal for them to be added on to the ad hoc list?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In this regard, the Agency for Care Effectiveness (ACE) uses the established Health Technology Assessments to evaluate the relative value of new drugs, compared to existing standards of care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In parallel, ACE also conducts value-based pricing negotiations to ensure drug prices are competitive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, the financing changes that we made have been a major step to incentivise drug companies to price drugs competitively so that their drugs would be eligible for subsidies, MSHL and IPs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And because of this, we have seen the promising results that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In respect of the Member's concern with regard to profiteering, actually, the Competition and Consumers Commission of Singapore also has levers to investigate all reports of anti-competitive behaviour and will take action against instances of anti-competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Member has also asked about the process and I would like to take some time to explain the assessments made by ACE I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: ACE assesses the clinical and cost effectiveness, using published methodologies that are in line with international best practices.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And it draws on clinical, epidemiological and health economic data, compare the incremental costs and incremental improvements in health benefits of the treatment relative to the existing standard of care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As part of this process, ACE consults MOH's Oncology Drugs Sub-Committee comprising local clinical experts from the public and private sectors to ascertain the clinical value of medicines and evaluation and the appropriate use of cancer therapies based on clinical evidence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Actually, the process has been put up on ACE's website.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Drug companies that wish to participate in this process would be able to time their applications accordingly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Funding implementation, typically, occurs within four to six months after a funding decision has been made.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But with timely evidence submission, high quality of clinical evidence and reasonable pricing proposals from the pharmaceutical companies, these will help to expedite it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Under this process, companies will be responsible for providing evidence submission to ACE, in parallel with HSA's regulatory approval process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This will bring funding decisions upstream, close to the point of market entry.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, they can do it ahead of time.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: By the time it comes in, we would already have allowed for it to be put in.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This minimises the time gap between HSA registration and inclusion into the drugs list.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, how does MOH ensure that insurers do not shortchange policyholders who have been dutifully paying their dues and what recourse do policyholders have to appeal against decisions from insurers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, are there guidelines on the premiums that insurers charge and what is the oversight on this?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While patients are allowed to change insurers, many, often, have little choice in changing insurers due to the coverage of existing conditions and risk loading.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: MOH and MAS work closely together in exercising regulatory oversight over Integrated Shield Plan (IP) insurers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: IP premiums are set, reviewed and adjusted by insurers based on commercial and actuarial considerations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Insurers may adjust premiums, taking into account the impact of the changes and their own claims experience and other factors.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, insurers have an incentive to help keep premiums competitive to attract and retain their policyholders.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, we hope all these changes, in the long run, will help to moderate premium increases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I also realised that I have not really addressed Dr Lim Wee Kiak's question about how patients can appeal for drugs to be considered for inclusion in CDL.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: They can refer the drug to ACE for ACE to make that assessment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We also note that, in the process where there are private patients, there is that opportunity for them to have direct referral to the public health institutions and this is where the assessment can also be made in respect of the appropriate treatment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There will also be subsidies available to that patient.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am not sure if my question on the introduction of a National Cancer Care Appeals Board was answered.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I understand from the ACE website, which the Senior Parliamentary Secretary just referred to, that it takes about 10 to 11 months from the time the pharmaceutical firms submit their pre-submission form to ACE to the time the Drug Advisory Committee (DAC) meets.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, for individual cancer patients, for whom time is of the essence, anything more than one week may be too long to wait for a decision on a drug subsidy approval.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can we, therefore, have a National Cancer Care Appeals Board which can make rigorous yet speedy decisions to subsidise drugs for these patients to get the life-saving drugs that they need?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: DAC can then take the necessary time to review the drug for inclusion into the Cancer Drug List to benefit patients at the national level.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: First off, we need to appreciate that when doctors actually make recommendations for treatment, it has to be on the basis of evidence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: All new and existing patients should be properly advised of the proven efficacy, side effects and costs of the available treatment options, including the financial implications of receiving a treatment that is not on CDL at the earliest opportunity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, we appreciate that by creating this drug list, there may be some patients who may require drugs outside the drug list and may face difficulties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This could include patients who already have tried drugs on CDL and found them ineffective for patients with contraindications to the drugs on the cancer list.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But there needs to be evidence of efficacy of the prescribed drug outside CDL.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In respect of those patients on a case-by-case basis, because what happens is that we have provided this lever where there is, actually, a direct referral to the public healthcare institutions (PHIs).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: They can, therefore, get discretionary funding that is available to them, thereby getting treatment at a far lower cost.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is through this referral that the doctors in the PHIs will then be able to assess the appropriate treatment that is meant for the patient.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The other question is related to the number.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The number of patients who will be affected by the cancer drug treatment changes is actually constantly fluctuating.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As patients drop in and out of treatments and, given the ongoing work, we are, actually, expanding the treatments on CDL.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And we have already said that, if they face difficulty and require non-CDL treatments, if they face difficulty affording the drugs, they can be referred to PHIs and they can get discretionary financial assistance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I know this is something that is challenging for patients who are facing these situations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But we need to look at the bigger picture and, that is, to reduce the ever-increasing drug prices.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With the moves that we have made, we have seen a reduction and this is something that we need to continue with.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have to help those who are not able to be covered under the list as much as we can.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We also then have to monitor the process as we go along to see and ensure that, in the long run, it will actually benefit more Singaporeans when all the drug prices can be moderated and are lowered because there is an incentive for the pharmaceutical companies to lower their prices.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I want to thank Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam for her replies and explaining the ACE process on how cancer drugs are evaluated, negotiated, because bringing the prices down really helps our Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I wanted to ask whether MOH will consider extending the negotiated price – or maybe more of a clarification – whether the negotiated price is also extended to benefit the private healthcare providers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is because ACE does tap on a committee that comprises public and private oncologists and, as parliamentarians, we would all know of a resident or someone we love who has cancer and is battling cancer and seeking private healthcare for reasons that we all understand, because they want to get well.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I just wanted a clarification whether that negotiated price also benefits our private healthcare providers to help our Singaporeans battling cancer.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will take this back and look into it and have extensive engagements with the industry.
